blocks.title: How cases are marked in this outline
body: **MAIN CASE** — a principal case: the casebook prints the opinion.
**NOTE CASE** — the casebook quotes or summarizes it in its notes.
**CITED ONLY** — the casebook just cites it, usually under a problem.
**★** = the case has its own slide(s) in class. [[Gray italic text]] = outside the class materials.

items: **Type of property** (goods, real estate, services, intellectual property);
**Nature of the rights transferred** (sale, lease, license, gift);

blocks.title: Speedy Offset prints & binds 500 art books
blocks.text: printing and binding are services in **manufacturing** goods, so goods predominate and **Article 2 applies**.

body: **§ 2-207(2):** between merchants, additional terms become part of the contract unless (a) the offer expressly limits acceptance to its terms; (b) they materially alter it; or (c) notification of objection has been or is given within a reasonable time.

blocks.name: Daitom, Inc. v. Pennwalt Corp.
blocks.facts: The buyer's purchase order and the seller's proposal had **different** terms on the time to sue and on warranties.
blocks.held: The different terms **knocked each other out**, and the UCC's own gap filler, the four-year period of § 2-725, governed.
blocks.why: the knock-out rule for **different** terms under § 2-207. [[Most courts follow it.]]

blocks.title: Two-part good faith test for a modification
body: A modification needs no consideration (§ 2-209(1)) but must be sought in good faith: (1) **objective** — would an ordinary merchant seek it?; (2) **subjective** — honesty in fact, with no extortion (§ 2-209 cmt. 2).

blocks.name: Roth Steel Products v. Sharon Steel Corp.
blocks.source: principal case, casebook pp. 105–110. Slide W2-S8.
blocks.facts: With demand booming, Sharon **threatened to stop selling Roth any steel** unless Roth agreed to a higher price than the contract set. Roth, unable to buy elsewhere, agreed and later sued.
blocks.held: The modification was **unenforceable**. Sharon had a legitimate reason to ask, but using a threat to stop performing was bad faith.
blocks.why: a legitimate reason to *ask* for a change isn't enough if you *extract* it by threatening to breach (§ 2-209 cmt. 2).

rows: As modified it's **$500+**, so it needs a record (§ 2-209(3)); the modification fails and the $400 deal stands.
Still under $500: **no writing needed**, and no consideration is required (§ 2-209(1)).

blocks.title: 10,000 widgets/month, delivery to buyer by the 5th

parts.label: (A)
parts.title: One late delivery accepted
parts.text: no course of performance (a single occasion), so the buyer keeps its claim if it gives timely notice.

parts.label: (B)
parts.title: Three late deliveries accepted
parts.text: an arguable **course of performance** (§ 1-303(a)) or a waiver the buyer can retract by reasonable notice (§ 2-209(5)).

items: **No consideration** is needed for a modification, but **good faith** is.
The statute of frauds applies to the contract **as modified** (§ 2-209(3)).

rows: On due delivery to the carrier

blocks.name: Windows, Inc. v. Jordan Panel Sys.
blocks.facts: Jordan ordered custom windows, which were damaged in transit.
blocks.held: In a shipment contract, risk passed to the buyer when the seller duly delivered the windows to the carrier (§ 2-509(1)(a)).

blocks.name: Ingram River Equip. v. Pott Indus.
blocks.facts: Ingram bought tank barges with heating coils to haul heavy petroleum products.
blocks.held: A fitness warranty could arise: the buyer's use need not be unique, only different from the goods' customary use.
blocks.why: draws the line between § 2-315 (particular purpose) and § 2-314 (ordinary purpose).

rows: A signed deal for a skid loader, silent on delivery: delivery is at the **seller's place of business** (§ 2-308), so the buyer breached by refusing to pick it up.
A history of the seller delivering is a **course of dealing** that fills the term, so the seller breached.
